intro: Grandma was a kid once. She rode a train with a paper ticket. She dialed a phone with her finger. Her school had a bell and a chalkboard. Some things she did, you still do. Some things are gone. Old photos and old objects are clues. They show us the past.

Our country has a past too. It has a flag with fifty stars. It has an eagle, a bell and a statue. It has holidays that remember people and big days. And it has citizens. That is you. In this unit you will learn how to read clues from long ago, and what it means to vote, help and speak up.
bigQuestion: How do we know about long ago, and what do we share as a country today?

timeline.t: Grandma is born. Her family cooks on a wood stove.
Grandma rides a train to Chicago with a paper ticket.
Grandma starts school. She writes on a slate with chalk.
Grandma's family gets a black phone with a dial.
Grandma has a baby. That baby is your mom.
Mom starts school. Her class has a chalkboard and a computer.
You are born. Your family takes a photo on a cell phone.
You start school. You say the Pledge and face the flag.
You open Grandma's shoebox and find the clues.
Someday you will show your old things to a kid and tell the story.

words.d: the time before now, like yesterday or long ago
the time right now
an object made or used by people long ago
a line that shows events in order, first to last
a thing that stands for something bigger, like the flag
a special day that a lot of people share
a member of a country or a community
to choose, with each person getting one choice

test.why: Yesterday is over. Time before now is the past.

test.q: Grandma's dial phone is a clue about what?
test.why: Old objects are artifacts. They are clues about the past.

test.q: How did people travel long ago, before cars?
test.why: Long ago, people walked, rode horses or rode in a wagon.

test.q: Which thing stayed the same from long ago to today?
test.why: Families cared for each other then and now. Phones and slates changed.

test.q: On a timeline, where does the first event go?
test.why: The first event goes on the left. The last goes on the right.

test.q: How many stars are on the flag, and why?
test.why: The flag has fifty stars. Each star is one state.

test.q: What does the Statue of Liberty stand for?
test.why: The Statue of Liberty is a symbol of freedom. Liberty means being free.

test.q: Which holiday is on the Fourth of July?
test.why: Independence Day is the Fourth of July, our country's birthday.

choices: She opened a house in Chicago
She led people out of slavery to freedom
test.why: Tubman ran away to be free, then went back to lead many others to freedom.

test.q: Which one is being a good citizen?
test.why: A good citizen helps others, votes fairly and speaks up kindly.

write.prompt: Pick one thing that changed from long ago to today, like travel, phones or school. Draw or write: what it was like long ago, what it is like now, and one clue that shows it changed.
tips: Start with your claim: "Travel changed a lot."
Give your evidence: a clue from the unit, like the wagon photo or Grandma's ticket.
Say why: what does the clue show?
Then name one thing that did NOT change.

title: Then and Now, and Our Country

chapters.title: Long Ago and Today
chapters.bigQuestion: How do we know what life was like long ago?

story.title: Grandma's Shoebox
story.kicker: A box under the bed holds a phone with a dial, an old ticket and a photo of a girl.
paragraphs: Maya is at Grandma's house in Chicago. She finds a shoebox under the bed. The box is dusty. Grandma smiles. "Open it," she says. "Those are my things from long ago."
Inside is a heavy black phone. It has a round dial with holes. No screen. No buttons. "You put your finger in a hole and turn it," Grandma says. "One number at a time. It took a while."

Under the phone is a paper ticket. It is small and yellow. It says "Chicago, Illinois." Grandma rode a train with it when she was six. Under the ticket is a photo. A girl stands in front of a school. She has braids.
"Who is that?" Maya asks. "That is me," says Grandma. "That was my school." Maya looks at the girl in the photo. Then she looks at Grandma. Same smile. Long ago, Grandma was a kid too.
story.think: What is one old thing in your home? What can it tell you about long ago?

lessons.title: Yesterday, Today, Tomorrow
lessons.mainIdea: The past is before now, the present is now, and the future is after now.
reading: Think about yesterday. What did you eat? What did you play? Yesterday is over. It is in the *past*. The past is all the time before now.
Now think about right now. You are reading. You are sitting. This is the *present*. The present is now, this very minute.
Tomorrow has not come yet. It is in the *future*. The future is the time after now. Long ago is the past. Someday is the future. Today is the present.

words.d: the time before now, like yesterday or long ago
the time right now
the time after now, like tomorrow or next year

look.title: Three Pictures of a Tree
look.text: Look at the first picture. A small girl plants a tiny tree. Look at the second picture. The girl is bigger. The tree is as tall as she is. Look at the third picture. The tree is huge. A grown woman sits under it with her own kids.
look.prompt: Which picture is the past? Which is the present? Which is the future?

check.q: Yesterday is in the what?
check.why: Yesterday is over. It is before now. That is the past.

check.q: What is the present?
check.why: The present is now, this very minute.

check.q: Tomorrow is in the what?
check.why: Tomorrow has not come yet. The time after now is the future.

lessons.title: Old Things Are Clues
lessons.mainIdea: Old photos and objects are clues that tell us about the past.
reading: We were not alive long ago. So how do we know about it? We look for *clues*. A clue is a thing that helps you figure something out. Old things are clues.
An old photo is a clue. Look at the clothes. Look at the cars. Look at the street. Each one tells you something. A photo is a piece of the past you can hold.
Grandma's dial phone is a clue too. It shows how people called each other. Old things like this are called *artifacts*. An artifact is an object made by people long ago.

words.d: a thing that helps you figure something out
an object made or used by people long ago

look.title: The Old Photo
look.text: Look at the photo. It is black and white, not color. A boy stands by a street. He wears short pants and a cap. Behind him is a car with big round lights and thin tires. A horse pulls a wagon down the same street.
look.prompt: Name three clues in the photo that show it was taken long ago.

check.q: What is an artifact?
choices: A new toy from the store
check.why: An artifact is an object made or used by people long ago.

check.q: How do we learn about the past?
choices: We wait for it to come
check.why: Old photos and old things are clues. They tell us about the past.

check.q: A photo shows a horse pulling a wagon on a street. What is that a clue for?
choices: The photo is from long ago
The photo is from the future
check.why: Long ago, horses pulled wagons on streets. That is a clue about the past.

lessons.title: Getting From Here to There
lessons.mainIdea: How people travel has changed a lot over time.
reading: Long ago, there were no cars. People walked. Or they rode a horse. Or a horse pulled their wagon. A trip to the next town took all day.
Then came trains. A train ran on rails. It carried many people fast. In Chicago, trains ran on tracks up in the air. People called it the "L." It is still there today.
Then came cars, buses and planes. Today a car ride to the next town takes minutes. A plane can cross the country in one day. *Travel* got faster and faster.

words.d: to go from one place to another place

look.title: The Same Trip
look.text: Look at the road to Grandma's town. Long ago, a boy rode there in a wagon. The horse walked all day. The boy got there at night. Today, a girl rides there in a car. She leaves after lunch. She gets there before dinner.
look.prompt: What changed? What stayed the same about the trip?

check.q: How did people travel long ago, before cars?
check.why: Long ago there were no cars. People walked or used horses and wagons.

check.q: What is the "L" in Chicago?
choices: A train on tracks up in the air
check.why: The "L" is a train that runs on tracks up in the air. It is still used today.

check.q: How did travel change over time?
check.why: Wagons were slow. Trains, cars and planes are much faster.

lessons.title: Cooking and Talking
lessons.mainIdea: Cooking and talking to far-away people changed as new tools were made.
reading: Long ago, people cooked on a wood *stove*. First you had to chop wood. Then you lit a fire. Then you waited for the stove to get hot. Cooking took a long time.
Today many people cook on a gas or electric stove. You turn a knob. It gets hot right away. Some people use a microwave. Dinner can be ready in minutes.
Talking changed too. Long ago, people wrote letters. A letter took days to arrive. Then came the phone with a dial. Today we use cell phones. We can talk or text right away.

words.d: a thing you cook food on

look.title: Two Kitchens
look.text: Look at the first kitchen. A big iron stove sits by the wall. A pile of wood sits next to it. A girl carries water in a bucket. Look at the second kitchen. A white stove has knobs. A microwave sits on the counter. Water comes from a sink.
look.prompt: Which kitchen is from long ago? How can you tell?

check.q: What did people burn in a stove long ago?
check.why: Long ago, people chopped wood and burned it in the stove.

check.q: How did people talk to far-away friends long ago?
choices: They called on a cell phone
check.why: Long ago there were no phones. People wrote letters that took days to arrive.

check.q: Why is cooking faster today?
check.why: Gas and electric stoves get hot right away. No wood to chop, no fire to build.

lessons.title: School Long Ago
lessons.mainIdea: Schools long ago had one room, one teacher and no computers.
reading: Long ago, many towns had a *one-room school*. All the kids sat in one room. Little kids and big kids. One teacher taught them all.
Kids wrote on small boards called slates. They used chalk. Then they wiped it off. There were no computers. There was no bus. Kids walked to school, even in snow.
Some things are the same. Kids learned to read. Kids did math. Kids played at recess. Ask a grown-up what their school was like. What did they have? What did they not have?

words.d: a school long ago where all the kids learned in one room

look.title: Ask Grandpa
look.text: Maya asks Grandpa about his school. He says, "We had a chalkboard, not a screen. We had a big bell that rang. We had no computers. But we had recess. And we had a mean kickball game."
look.prompt: What is one thing that changed? What is one thing that stayed the same?

check.q: What did kids write on long ago?
check.why: Kids wrote on small boards called slates. They used chalk and wiped it off.

check.q: In a one-room school, who taught the little kids and the big kids?
check.why: All the kids sat in one room. One teacher taught them all.

check.q: What is one thing that stayed the same at school?
check.why: Kids learned to read long ago too. Buses and computers are new.

lessons.title: A Town in One Hundred Years
lessons.mainIdea: A town can change a lot in one hundred years, and old maps and photos show how.
reading: Picture a small town one hundred years ago. It has a dirt road. It has a store, a church and a school. Farms are all around it. Horses stand by the store.
Now picture the same town today. The road is paved. There are more houses. There is a gas station. There is a big store. Cars are parked where the horses stood.
How do we know the town *changed*? We look at old maps. We look at old photos. We count the people. Chicago was a small town once. Now it is a big city.

words.d: to become different from before

look.title: How Many People Lived in Chicago
look.prompt: When did Chicago have the fewest people? When did it have the most?

check.q: What was the road like in the town one hundred years ago?
check.why: The old town had a dirt road. Today the road is paved.

check.q: How can we tell a town changed?
choices: We look at old maps and photos
check.why: Old maps and photos are clues. They show how a place looked before.

check.q: Chicago in 1850 had about how many people?
check.why: The chart shows about thirty thousand people in 1850. It was a small town.

lessons.title: Families, Play and Food
lessons.mainIdea: Some things stay the same over time, like families, play and eating together.
reading: Not everything changes. Long ago, kids lived with families. Families cared for each other. That is still true today. Families are a thing that stayed the *same*.
Kids played long ago too. They played tag. They jumped rope. They played with dolls and balls. Toys look different now. But kids still love to play.
Families ate together long ago. They ate bread, soup and corn. Today we still eat bread and soup and corn. The food came from a farm then. It comes from a farm now.

words.d: not different; just like before

look.title: Jump Rope, Then and Now
look.text: Look at the old photo. Three girls jump rope on a sidewalk. They wear long dresses. Look at the new photo. Three girls jump rope on a sidewalk. They wear shorts and sneakers. Both groups are laughing.
look.prompt: What changed in the two photos? What stayed the same?

check.q: Which thing stayed the same over time?
check.why: Long ago and today, families care for each other. Phones and wagons changed.

check.q: Did kids play long ago?
choices: Yes, they played tag and jumped rope
check.why: Kids long ago played tag, jumped rope and played with balls.

check.q: Where did food come from long ago and today?
check.why: Food came from a farm then. It still comes from a farm now.

lessons.title: A Timeline of My Life
lessons.mainIdea: A timeline puts events in order from first to last.
reading: A *timeline* is a line with events on it. The first thing goes on the left. The last thing goes on the right. It shows what came first and what came next.
Make a timeline of your life. First: you were born. Next: you learned to walk. Next: you lost a tooth. Next: you started school. Draw each one on the line.
A family timeline is longer. Ask a grown-up. When were they born? When did they start school? Put their events on the line. Put yours after. Now you see the past and the present together.

words.d: a line that shows events in order, first to last
something that happens

look.title: Maya's Timeline
look.text: Look at Maya's timeline. On the left it says "Born." Next it says "First steps." Next it says "Baby brother." Next it says "Lost a tooth." On the right it says "Started first grade."
look.prompt: Which event came first? Which came last? What might Maya add next?

check.q: On a timeline, where does the first event go?
check.why: The first thing goes on the left. The last thing goes on the right.

check.q: Which event would come first on your timeline?
check.why: You were born before you did anything else. It goes first.

check.q: Why ask a grown-up for a family timeline?
choices: They know events from before you were born
check.why: Grown-ups lived in the past before you. They can tell you what happened.

review.q: Long ago is in the what?
review.why: Long ago is before now. That is the past.
An old photo shows clothes, cars and streets from long ago. It is a clue.

review.q: Before cars, how did people travel far?
review.why: Long ago, people walked or rode horses. A horse pulled the wagon.

review.q: What did kids use to write on in a one-room school?
review.why: Kids wrote on slates with chalk. There were no computers.

review.q: Which one stayed the same from long ago to today?
choices: The kind of phone we use
review.why: Kids played long ago and play today. Phones and stoves changed.

review.q: On a timeline, the last event goes where?
review.why: First goes on the left. Last goes on the right.

chapters.title: Symbols, Holidays and Being a Citizen
chapters.bigQuestion: What do we share as a country, and what is my job in it?

story.title: The Class Pet Gets a Name
story.kicker: A new hamster needs a name. Twenty-two kids have ideas. How will they choose?
paragraphs: Room 12 has a new class pet. It is a small brown hamster. It runs on its wheel. It stuffs seeds in its cheeks. Everyone loves it. But it has no name.
"I want Peanut!" says Jae. "No, Biscuit!" says Ana. "Rocket!" says Sam. Soon everyone is shouting. Ms. Ortiz raises her hand. The room gets quiet. "We will vote," she says.
Ms. Ortiz writes three names on the board: Peanut, Biscuit, Rocket. Each kid gets one slip of paper. Each kid writes one name. No peeking. The slips go in a jar.
Ms. Ortiz counts. Peanut gets six. Rocket gets seven. Biscuit gets nine. "Biscuit wins," she says. Jae wanted Peanut. But he shrugs. "That was fair," he says. "Hi, Biscuit."
story.think: Why was voting a fair way to pick the name? What else could the class have done?

lessons.title: Stars and Stripes
lessons.mainIdea: The flag has fifty stars for fifty states and thirteen stripes for the first thirteen states.
reading: Look at the *flag* of the United States. It is red, white and blue. It has stars and stripes. A flag is a *symbol*. A symbol is a thing that stands for something bigger.
Count the stars. There are fifty. Each star stands for one state. Illinois is one star. Our country has fifty states, so the flag has fifty stars.
Count the stripes. There are thirteen. Seven are red. Six are white. They stand for the first thirteen states. Those states started our country long ago.

words.d: a piece of cloth with colors and shapes that stands for a country
a thing that stands for something bigger

look.title: Count the Flag
look.cite: The flag of the United States
look.prompt: What does each star stand for? What do the stripes stand for?

check.q: How many stars are on the flag?
check.why: The flag has fifty stars. Each star is one state.

check.q: What do the thirteen stripes stand for?
check.why: The stripes stand for the first thirteen states that started our country.

check.q: What is a symbol?
choices: A thing that stands for something bigger
check.why: A symbol stands for something bigger. The flag stands for our country.

lessons.title: The Pledge Is a Promise
lessons.mainIdea: The Pledge of Allegiance is a promise to be loyal to our country.
reading: Many schools say the *Pledge* in the morning. Kids stand up. They face the flag. They put a hand on their heart. They say the words together.
A pledge is a promise. The Pledge says we will be *loyal* to our country. Loyal means you stick with something and care for it. It says our country is one country, all together.
The Pledge ends with "liberty and justice for all." Liberty means being free. Justice means being fair. For all means everyone. That is the promise.

words.d: a promise you say out loud
to stick with something and care for it

look.title: The Words of the Pledge
look.text: I pledge allegiance to the Flag of the United States of America, and to the Republic for which it stands, one Nation under God, indivisible, with liberty and justice for all.
look.cite: The Pledge of Allegiance, as set in United States law
look.prompt: Find the words "liberty" and "justice." What do they mean?

check.q: What is a pledge?
check.why: A pledge is a promise. The Pledge is a promise to our country.

check.q: What does liberty mean?
check.why: Liberty means being free.

check.q: Who is the promise of justice for?
check.why: The Pledge says "justice for all." All means everyone.

lessons.title: The Bald Eagle
lessons.mainIdea: The bald eagle is a symbol of our country because it is strong and free.
reading: A big bird flies over a river. It has a white head. It has a yellow beak. Its wings are wide. It is a *bald eagle*. It is not really bald. Its head feathers are white.
Long ago, the leaders of our country picked the eagle as a symbol. The eagle is strong. It flies high and free. Eagles live only in North America. That made it a good pick.
Look for the eagle. It is on coins. It is on dollar bills. It is on the seal of the president. Bald eagles live in Illinois too. You can see them by the Mississippi River in winter.

words.d: a big bird with a white head that is a symbol of the United States

look.title: Look at a Quarter
look.text: Take out a quarter. Look at the back. On many quarters, an eagle spreads its wings. It has a strong beak and sharp claws. Now look at a one-dollar bill. Turn it over. There is the eagle again, holding a branch and arrows.
look.prompt: Why do you think the eagle is on our money?

check.q: Why is the bald eagle a symbol of our country?
check.why: The eagle is strong and flies high and free. Leaders picked it long ago.

check.q: Is a bald eagle really bald?
choices: Yes, it has no feathers on its head
No, its head feathers are white
Yes, it is bald all over
check.why: The eagle's head feathers are white. It only looks bald from far away.

check.q: Where can you find a picture of the eagle?
check.why: The eagle is on coins, dollar bills and the president's seal.

lessons.title: A Bell and a Statue
lessons.mainIdea: The Liberty Bell and the Statue of Liberty are symbols of freedom.
reading: In Philadelphia there is an old bell. It is big and made of metal. It has a crack. It is the *Liberty Bell*. Long ago, it rang for our new country. Today it does not ring. But people come to see it.
In New York there is a giant green *statue*. A statue is a figure made of metal or stone. This one is a woman. She holds a torch up high. She is the Statue of Liberty.
France gave the statue to our country as a gift. That was more than one hundred years ago. Ships full of people sailed past her. She was the first thing they saw. She stands for freedom.

words.d: a figure of a person or animal made of metal or stone
a cracked old bell in Philadelphia that is a symbol of freedom

look.title: The Torch
look.text: Look at the statue. She is taller than a tall building. She wears a crown with seven points. In one hand she holds a book. In the other hand she holds a torch high in the air. A torch is a light. Her torch says: come this way.
look.prompt: Why do you think she holds a light up high?

check.q: Where is the Liberty Bell?
check.why: The Liberty Bell is in Philadelphia. People go there to see it.

check.q: What does the Statue of Liberty hold up high?
check.why: She holds a torch up high in one hand. A torch is a light.

check.q: Who gave the statue to our country?
check.why: France gave the statue as a gift more than one hundred years ago.

lessons.title: Days for Great Leaders
lessons.mainIdea: Some holidays remember people, like Martin Luther King Jr. and our presidents.
reading: A *holiday* is a special day. Some holidays remember a person. In January we have Martin Luther King Jr. Day. Dr. King worked so that all people would be treated fairly, no matter their skin color.
Dr. King gave speeches. He led marches. He did not fight with fists. He used words. He said all kids should be able to play and learn together. Many people listened.
In February we have Presidents' Day. It remembers George Washington, our first president. It remembers Abraham Lincoln too. Lincoln lived in Illinois. Both were born in February.

words.d: a special day that a lot of people share
the leader of our country

look.title: A March
look.text: Look at the old photo. Thousands of people walk down a wide street. They carry signs. Some signs say "Jobs." Some say "Freedom." Dr. King walks in front. No one is fighting. They are walking together to ask for fair treatment.
look.prompt: What did the people want? How did they ask for it?

check.q: What did Dr. King work for?
check.why: Dr. King worked so all people would be treated fairly, no matter their skin color.

check.q: How did Dr. King ask for change?
check.why: He used words. He gave speeches and led marches.

check.q: Presidents' Day remembers which two presidents most?
check.why: Presidents' Day remembers George Washington and Abraham Lincoln. Both were born in February.

lessons.title: Days for Our Country
lessons.mainIdea: Independence Day is our country's birthday, and Veterans Day thanks people who served.
reading: On the Fourth of July we have *Independence Day*. It is our country's birthday. On July 4, 1776, our leaders signed a paper. It said we were our own country. That was about 250 years ago.
People wave flags. They have parades. They watch fireworks at night. In Chicago, boats fill the lake. Families have picnics. It is a big party for the whole country.
On November 11 we have Veterans Day. A *veteran* is a person who served in the military. That means the army, the navy and more. We say thank you to them. Some kids have a veteran in their family.

words.d: the Fourth of July, our country's birthday
a person who served in the military

look.title: Two Parades
look.text: Look at the first parade. It is July. It is hot. Kids wave small flags. A band plays. At night, fireworks boom. Look at the second parade. It is November. It is cold. Old men and women in uniforms walk slowly. People clap and say thank you.
look.prompt: Which parade is Independence Day? Which is Veterans Day? How do you know?

check.q: When is Independence Day?
check.why: Independence Day is the Fourth of July. It is our country's birthday.

check.q: What is a veteran?
choices: A person who served in the military
check.why: A veteran served in the army, navy or another part of the military.

check.q: What happened on July 4, 1776?
choices: Leaders signed a paper saying we were our own country
check.why: On that day, leaders signed a paper. It said we were our own country.

lessons.title: People Who Made a Difference
lessons.mainIdea: Lincoln, Tubman, Chavez and Addams each helped other people and made things fairer.
reading: Abraham Lincoln lived in Illinois. He became president. Back then, some people were held as *slaves*. A slave is a person who is owned by someone else and is not free. Lincoln worked to end slavery.
Harriet Tubman was a slave. She ran away to be free. Then she went back. Again and again. She led many other people to freedom. It was very dangerous.
Cesar Chavez helped farm workers get fair pay. Jane Addams opened a big house in Chicago. Poor families came there to learn and get help. Each of these people saw a problem and helped.

words.d: a person who is owned by someone else and is not free
treating people the right way, with everyone getting a chance

look.title: Jane Addams's House
look.text: Look at the big house on Halsted Street in Chicago. It is 1889. Kids play in a yard. Inside, a mom learns to read. A nurse checks a baby. A boy paints a picture. Jane Addams walks through, saying hello to everyone.
look.prompt: Who came to the house? How did it help them?

check.q: What did Abraham Lincoln work to end?
check.why: Lincoln was president. He worked to end slavery.

check.q: What did Harriet Tubman do after she got free?
choices: She went back to lead others to freedom
check.why: Tubman went back again and again to lead other people to freedom.

check.q: What did Jane Addams do in Chicago?
choices: She opened a house to help poor families
check.why: Jane Addams opened a big house where poor families could learn and get help.

lessons.title: Vote, Help, Speak Up
lessons.mainIdea: A good citizen votes, helps others and speaks up when something is wrong.
reading: A *citizen* is a member of a country or a community. You are a citizen of your class. A good citizen helps. Pick up trash. Share. Help a friend who fell.
A good citizen *votes*. To vote is to choose. Each person gets one vote. The choice with the most votes wins. Grown-ups vote for leaders. Room 12 voted for Biscuit.
A good citizen speaks up. If something is not fair, say so. Say it kindly. Say it clearly. Dr. King spoke up. Jane Addams spoke up. You can too.

words.d: a member of a country or a community
to choose, with each person getting one choice

look.title: The Playground Problem
look.text: Only the big kids get the swings at recess. The little kids never get a turn. Nia thinks that is not fair. She could stay quiet. She could yell at the big kids. Or she could tell the teacher and ask the class to make a rule.
look.prompt: What should Nia do? What would a good citizen do?

check.q: What does it mean to vote?
choices: To choose, one vote per person
check.why: To vote is to choose. Each person gets one vote. Most votes wins.

check.q: Something at school is not fair. What does a good citizen do?
check.why: A good citizen speaks up when something is wrong. Say it kindly and clearly.

check.q: Which one is being a good citizen?
choices: Picking up trash on the playground
check.why: A good citizen helps. Picking up trash helps everyone.

review.q: What does each star on the flag stand for?
review.why: The flag has fifty stars for fifty states.
A pledge is a promise. The Pledge is a promise to be loyal to our country.

review.q: Which bird is a symbol of our country?
review.why: The bald eagle is strong and free. It is on coins and dollar bills.

review.q: Which holiday is our country's birthday?
review.why: Independence Day is July 4. Our country began on July 4, 1776.
Abraham Lincoln lived in Illinois before he became president. Dr. King was not a president.

review.q: Room 12 picked a name by voting. Why was that fair?
review.why: Each kid got one vote. The name with the most votes won.
